translations.text: WHEN, brothers, the laws preached to us about mercy, when the discourse turned to love for the poor and hospitality,
I saw the longing of you all, praised your zeal, and blessed your willingness, for I saw you eagerly receiving the heavenly word like thirsty ground.
And you know this for certain: what rain is to the earth, the word of God is to souls.
And just as rain stirs the earth to produce plants, so the word of God urges souls to bear the fruit of divinely inspired self-control.
Therefore I consider blessed Moses a witness to the enlivening and fruitful power of divine teaching.
In his holy, great, and glorious blessing, he declares: “Let them await my utterance as rain, and let my words descend like dew.”
And so that no one should think he attributed the abundance of such divine speech to himself, he immediately adds: “For I will proclaim the name of the Lord.”
I praise you, brothers, because you are not intent merely on hearing words, but store within yourselves the beauty of the thoughts expressed in them.
Like a wise bee entering the immortal and spiritual [?] of the holy Scriptures, bright with the flowers of devotion to God,
let each of you make the honey of divine sayings in the hidden hives of your souls.
Just as the bee and the nature and strength of bees come from flowers, and enjoyment must come from the bees’ labors,
so the flower and strength of devotion to God come from the divine Scriptures, and the enjoyment of devotion to God
comes from the labor of the virtuous; he made within souls such honeycomb [?] of the divine sayings.
And blessed David, having tasted how good devotion to God is, cried aloud in the melodies of the psalms: “Your words are sweeter to my palate than honey to my mouth.”
But I do not praise your willingness as much as I marvel at the father’s freedom from envy.
He blossoms with divine love and shines with heavenly grace; he waters the church so abundantly and in such a way, and makes this city of God rejoice.
It is timely to speak the words of the Psalm: “The streams of the river make the city of God rejoice.” He pours forth such holy and clear streams, yet does not disdain the few drops of our words.
Such a cloud, [?] with heavenly rains, does not shrink from receiving the slight murmur of our tongue, but praises it along with you.
Before you do, through the intercession of his holy prayers, he grants us speakers the ability to speak, and the listeners the willingness to listen.
And he praises what is his own as though it belonged to another, imitating his Lord Christ, who received what came from the prophets and praised the prophet’s proclamation.

He himself spoke through the mouth of Isaiah the prophet, and he himself gave voice to the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Yet, receiving what was his own as though it came from the prophet, he says to the Jews:
“Hypocrites, Isaiah spoke well about you.” It was not Isaiah who spoke well, but you who spoke well through Isaiah.
And so did all the prophets. Zechariah also bears witness: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets.”
It was not the mouths of the prophets, but the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Just as a reed pen writes not what it wishes, but what the hand commands,
so the tongue of the prophets spoke not what it wished, but what the abundance of the Holy Spirit commanded.
For this reason they rightly consider David’s cry beautiful: “My tongue is like the reed [?] of a swift-writing scribe.”
And now may this wondrous father himself, through his holy prayers, grant us an abundance of words; may he hear and praise the very thing that prayer gives.
And now, since we have such a father, and the feast is just beginning, come: upheld by his holy prayers, let us take flight and raise our minds to the height of the glory of the Only Begotten.
Not so that we might comprehend the greatness of his honor, but so that we may eagerly approach him in love.
For nothing can comprehend the honor of the Only Begotten, neither the breadth of words nor the qualities of minds. For he surpasses and goes beyond every mind and every thought.
And the blessed David expressed this figuratively, saying, “A person will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted.”
The more someone reflects on these words, the higher above him he finds the knowledge of the truth.
And now let us speak of the goodness of the Only Begotten from the present reading.
The fountain of wisdom uses parables, who said through David’s mouth, “I will open my mouth in parables.”
And he tells an example and a parable full of power, which, judging by its words, seems to contain nothing resembling his goodness.
“Which of you has a friend and goes to him at midnight and says, ‘Friend, give me three loaves of bread, for a friend of mine has arrived from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’?
“And he answers and says, ‘The doors are shut, and my children are with me in bed. Do not trouble me; I cannot get up and give you anything.’
And what did he add to this? “Truly I tell you, even if he will not give because of his friendship, nevertheless, because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him more than he wanted.
“And I tell you: ask, and you will receive.” And what resemblance does the parable bear to his goodness?
For he is sleepless by nature, while this man lies idle in bed. He is not overcome by sluggishness, while this man is a slave to sluggishness and sleep.
And now, what corresponding likeness does the parable wish to show? He adds to the same passage, “You too should ask, just as that man persisted in asking the sleeper.”
Do you, then, also sleep? Did not the prophets cry out about you, “The guardian of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep”? And now, what corresponding likeness does your parable wish to make clear?
The words of the Giver of Life customarily present corresponding things through similar things, and show their opposites through contrary things.
He makes this clear in the other parable as well, when he once wished, by means of a contrary example, to display his own abundantly flowing goodness,
his abundant and overflowing gifts, and his inexhaustible generosity. He brought forward an example of this kind, as we have just heard.
But first let this be examined, so that what he wishes to show may become clear. Although the example is not similar, the Savior wishes to say this:

that if the man persuaded someone enslaved to sleep, beset by sluggishness, and discouraged behind closed doors, to persevere and provide for those who had arrived late, and through his endurance overcame that man’s irritation,

will not those who truly approach the nature that is never sluggish persuade it to persevere and provide for those who have arrived late? I mean that nature which neither feels irritation nor is enslaved to sleep.
And who would take up arms and fight against such thoughts? And so that you may learn with certainty that he taught the opposite by means of a contrary example,
a little farther down he uses the same kind of example, to show the opposite by means of a contrary example.

Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? And if he asks for a fish, will he give him a snake instead of a fish? And if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion instead of an egg?
After explaining the higher things through a human comparison, he then says, “If you, who are evil,
know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father, the heavenly Father, give good things to those who ask him!”
Do you see how, by comparing something with its opposite, he demonstrated the opposite of it?
He also uses a parable of this kind elsewhere, as I said earlier. I consider it important to explain what it is and what force it has.
“There was a judge,” he says, “in a certain city, who neither feared God nor respected people.” A widow continually persisted in pleading with him, but he never settled anything.
For because of his harshness and his failure to acknowledge God, he would not respond to her pleading entreaties. But her persistence overcame his savage harshness.
The unjust judge says to himself, “Though I do not fear God or respect people, at least because she keeps troubling me, I will secure justice for her.” He tells this parable.
But the giver of life wished to demonstrate the opposite by means of its opposite, and immediately adds the following:
“See,” he says, “what the unjust judge said.” If perseverance and the widow’s persistence were enough to persuade the unjust and cruel [?],
will the persistence of those who persevere not be enough to incline the kind and abundantly compassionate Father, the Lord who loves humanity, to hear their pleas and show mercy?
He demonstrated this through that parable, and now he explains the same thing: “And I say to you: Ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened to you.”
Follow the example of the friend who knocked at the door and said, “Friend, open to me.” You too should knock, and it will be opened. Seek, and you will find.
But when you ask God, bear in mind [?] what you ought to ask and what sort of person you are asking. For many people form various notions of God in their prayers.

When they plead concerning their own sins, they want God to be kind and loving toward humanity. But when they call for vengeance against those who wrong them, they want him to be a stern, severe, and just judge.
When someone stands in prayer on his own behalf, he presents words of pleading and entreaty that can persuade God. “I beg you,” he says, “Lord, have mercy on me, unworthy as I am.
You are kind, generous, and loving toward humanity; you do not look upon sins, and you overlook offenses. If you scrutinize acts of lawlessness, who can endure before you?
Deal with me according to your mercy.” They say all this when they offer prayers on their own behalf.

But when someone, distressed by his enemy, comes to stand in prayer, he forgets such words and turns his entreaties toward another purpose. “Lord,” he says, “you are a just judge, and evil people are not pleasing to you.
Take vengeance on my enemies, for you are a righteous judge. Do not be patient with those who oppress me, but, as a just judge, demand justice.”
When I judge you, you want me to be kind and generous; but when I judge your enemy, you want me to be just and impartial.
Have you forgotten your first prayers? Did you not call upon me as one who is kind? Did you not seek to persuade me as one who loves humanity? Did you not plead with me as one who is patient?
How can this be? Must I somehow divide myself according to your wishes and barter justice to suit your preferences?

But it is not possible for you to receive only good things from my generosity, while your enemies receive only sentences of justice from my righteous judgment. For the generous one is generous toward everyone.
Perhaps, while you stand in prayer against your enemies, you provoke the judge to anger against yourself. How?
The just judge examines your case and another person’s equally. If you invoke him as a just judge against your enemies, you must also stir the judge up against yourself.
But if you appeal to him as a benefactor on your own behalf, then he will be a benefactor to everyone, even if you do not wish it.
Therefore, anyone who stands in prayer must ask for what is pleasing to God. It is fitting to ask for whatever God takes pleasure in.
For if the Savior, when he said, “Father, if it is at all possible, let this cup pass from me,” immediately added,
“But not as I will, but as you will,” do you, an unruly man, choose your own wishes instead of taking refuge in his will?
But now let us bring the discourse to this point. For I know that this is precisely what you were asking for, and I see you crowded together, cramped, and eager to hear the discourse.
But take comfort, for Isaiah has arrived and will give you encouragement: “Bear with these hardships, you who are eager to listen.”
He spoke well; listen well, all of you, cramped in body but with your spirits enlarged and refreshed. For this discomfort here will bring you relief from many hardships.
Those who endure sweat on their bodies for God’s sake dispel all the pains of sin. For if sweat produced by the body dispels pain, then such sweat,
which pours out for God’s sake and for the sake of his words, from the spring of your longing to hear what you have come to hear—will it not wash away all sins together?
But let us proceed to what lies before us, for I know that you are asking for the remainder of the discourse.
Many ask eagerly, as friends would, while many hunt for pretexts and think of finding fault.
For the disparagement of the many who wish to find fault with us has not escaped our notice: they say that we left the discourse incomplete, without examining the matter.
But I am astonished at such people, not at their slander but at their untimeliness. You find fault as though you had made a loan and had not received repayment.
When you asked for the discourse, was I [?] about giving the explanation? Did someone else put the question forward, and did I reject it?
I made the promise of my own accord, and I myself forgot. If that is so, blame the frailties of my nature, and do not reproach the exposition of the discourse.
For even if the [?] had eluded us, even then the weakness of the discourse would not destroy the strength of the argument.
For the claims of truth are not banished by my inability, since the grounds for the matters before us are themselves clear.
But the abundance of these words I have spoken scattered our thoughts this way and that, drawing them away from the question that lay before us.
And now, what I left unfinished unwillingly then, I will willingly repay now as a debt.
Yet even as I repay it, I am again apprehensive, for I see in you a new and wonderful intoxication:
an intoxication that does not make the mind dull, but stimulates the memory more and more. You all know that the effect of drunkenness is to dull the attention.
But you, brothers, the more you become intoxicated with the divine word, the more you drive dullness away from your attention and plant divine memories in its place.
And this is what is astonishing: cupbearers become drunk and are weighed down by the excess of their service,
but you, who have drained so many vessels of the divine word, are still thirsty after your intoxication and insistently ask for what remains.

Indeed, one gets to hear the words of those who are spiritually drunk. “What is the cup?” they say. “The cup was left unexplained; he did not explain the cup; he did not discharge his debt concerning the account of the cup.”
I love you because you long for Christ’s cup. I love you because you ask for what remains. I love you because, for the sake of that beautiful drunkenness, you do not wish to lose even one cup.
And quite rightly so. For at a bodily feast, someone who passes over a single cup out of moderation is admirable;
but in divine rejoicing and at the heavenly table, nothing is left out of those things that draw one into the drunkenness of delight.
Rather, the one who is at once satisfied and hungry, drunk and thirsty, is the one who will truly be filled with eternal salvation.

And now I pronounce blessed both those who speak and those who listen: you who listen, because you thirst to hear, just as the Savior says, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled”;
and those who speak, because they sound forth divine teaching into living ears. Blessed are those who speak into the ears of listeners. And now let us turn to the saying.
“Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” This saying is full of many questions and brings many severe afflictions upon the heretics,
not because it was spoken wrongly, but because they wrongly understand the words, “if it is possible.”

Some supposed that certain unfailing decrees, which could not be transgressed, were proclaimed from the body [?]: namely, fate and allotment and the necessity attached to what is fabulously called one’s nativity, as though something were thus allotted to each person from birth.

And some dishonor the dignity of the Only-begotten in another way: they fasten a slavish obedience of the Son to the Father onto him. For, they say, he was under the Father’s authority, and for that reason he offered such supplications.

What argument is suitable for us to resolve these questions? What thoughts will suffice to unravel the many-voiced fables of the heretics? It would not be possible [?] to learn from anywhere else than from the truth itself.

Come now, let us ascend to the divine heights, there to the saving work of the heavenly Giver of life, who does everything and speaks all things not only in keeping with the dignity that befits him, but also in keeping with the saving provision appropriate for us.
And to put it briefly—for I always like to speak concisely and encompass much in few words—the Giver of life knew beforehand

that the sufferings were absolutely necessary. He knew beforehand that the cross was established for the salvation of the world, that death would be rebuked, and that resurrection would be brought about.

And he knew this so well that he told the disciples beforehand, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of sinners, and they will scourge him and crucify him, and on the third day he will rise.”
This is the utterance of God, who knows future things beforehand. It is God who anticipates the actual experience of events; it is God who directs human affairs with knowledge.
Then Peter answers him about this, moved with pity for his body: “Far be it, Lord,” he says. “Let this not happen to you.”

And what did the Giver of life do in response? He grew angry at this untimely pity; he reproached this misplaced concern: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not think the things of God, but the things of human beings.”
Approach the saying rightly. Examine it yourself and keep watch over it. For if you attend only to the words, you greatly undermine the Giver of life:
you accuse him not only of weakness, but also of instability in his intentions.
O beneficent Lord, when Peter wished that it should be far from you to go up onto the cross, you rebuked him.
And now do you yourself ask for the very thing for which you blamed him—a thing that was unfitting not only for [?], but even for a steadfast human being?

Who would praise a general who makes many promises before the battle and boldly shouts defiance at the enemy, but turns to flight when the battle lines clash and disgraces his strength through cowardice?
Before Christ came to his sufferings, he said to the one who tried to dissuade him from suffering, “Get away from me, Satan, for you are thinking not of the things of God, but of human things.”
And would he who considered such counsel unworthy of God actually accept that same counsel for himself and pray for it?
Oh, the foolishness—or rather, the arrogance—of those who serve mere words, recklessly dare everything, and presume to interpret divine things in conflicting ways,
and refuse to understand that, by accepting the words alone, they portray him as lower not only than the Father,
as they are eager to do, but also as inferior to many wise and righteous people, and as entirely lacking even human steadfastness.
What wise or righteous person, or indeed any human being whose courage is attested, would deny his own virtue and dishonor the strength he had promised and previously boasted of?
Who would behave so cowardly and inopportunely as to dare and undertake one thing, but think another and shrink back when put to the test?
He who threatened death with death and proclaimed the good news of the resurrection—how could he himself shrink from the cross?
I have said all this to rebuke those who serve words, dishonor the Lord, and sell the truth.
Now, what would anyone wish to demonstrate against the contradiction between the words, when the truth is always found to agree with itself?
And how can any agreement of the truth with the conflict between the words be understood at all?
The words do indeed conflict with one another, but the agreement of the divine utterances remains firm.
Now I must explain the solution to the question before us with a diligent disposition, and you must listen with minds eager to learn.
When the Lord approached his crucifixion, at the completion of the entire divine plan, the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, knew beforehand
that many heretics would rise against the truth, separate the divine sufferings from him, and falsely declare his deeds foreign to him;
especially those who share their name with error—I mean the disciples of the Manichaeans—who even dared to say that Christ’s sufferings were a mere shadow and an illusion before the eyes,

as though he had not even assumed a body, the cross was only an appearance, the body was merely a shadow and a likeness, and everything accomplished was an appearance, a shadow, an illusion, and something merely before the eyes.
Because of such heretical error—I mean that of the disciples of the Manichaeans—in order to silence the mouths of the heretics beforehand and make it clear
that he put on this body, which is subject to many needs, which shrinks from sufferings, which trembles before the power of death, and which is troubled and trembles at the end of life,
he says, “Now my soul is troubled”; and again, “My soul is sorrowful to the point of death”; and again, “If it is possible, Father, let this cup pass from me.”

If these things were a shadow, a mere appearance, and an illusion, why was he troubled? If the things being done were merely appearances, why did he shrink back? For no one fears a shadow or is troubled by mere appearances.
Would you like me also to demonstrate the truth more firmly from an account of ours? Angels entered Sodom. In appearance they looked like men, but by nature they were angels.
The Sodomites dared to force them, as though they were men, into filth and shameful depravity.
Now, what did the angels do? Since they knew that they had no body that could be subjected to violence, they were not troubled.
Instead, the angels’ nature remained undisturbed and suffered no turmoil from the storm of bodily passions.
But Lot, because he considered them righteous men, was troubled lest they suffer some violence. He pleaded with those raging men:
“I beg you,” he said, “do not wrong these men, because they have come under my roof. I will give you my own offspring. Take my daughters and do whatever you wish.”
Oh, the earnestness of his hospitality! He was prepared to give his own in place of others to [?]. Lot was troubled as a human being.
But the angels’ nature suffered no disturbance. For they went outside with great authority and snatched away the one who could suffer violence.
And those who raged with such mad fury—or rather, with such godless shamelessness—they struck with blindness.
They wandered about all night, looking for the door, but could not find it. For those who used their sight for evil were rightly and justly blinded.

And why was all this said, since the preceding discussion has nothing in common with the present one? It was to show that where there is an outward appearance, there is no fear, but where there is a real body, there are fear and sorrow.
But to make entirely clear why he spoke those words, the life-giving Savior cut off the heretics’ reasoning and established the teachings of truth by saying to the apostles:
“My spirit is willing, but my flesh is weak.” He attributes the weakness to his own flesh, while you attribute the sufferings to his divinity.
But if you do not strive to discover the meaning of the words, you will find that you have insulted the Lord.
For you not only establish what you suppose—that he offered prayers to the Father, and that the one who prays is inferior to the one whom he entreats—but I will say something still clearer:
If you attend only to the words, you make him inferior not only to the Father but even to his own apostles.
Just as they badly misinterpret the saying, “I speak nothing on my own, but my Father gave me a command about what I should say and what I should speak,” so they also misinterpret this.
Here let apostolic authority come forward on my behalf and silence the mouths of these madmen.
Paul says, “Concerning virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give advice.” And he shows that the heretics’ teachings are truly very base.
If Paul has authority to act freely without a command from God, does Christ not have authority to speak without the Father’s commands?
Likewise here, by comparison with the apostles’ courage, the heretics’ error is exposed, [?] that the Lord’s utterance is far inferior to the apostles’ dignity.
But as I have already said many times, if you attend only to the words, nothing more is accomplished.
But if we grasp their meaning, the truth remains undefiled—or rather, we ourselves remain undefiled, for the truth is never [?].

Now, if you pay no attention to the interpretation but attend only to the words, you will find Christ losing courage and speaking in a way far beneath not only his own dignity but also the apostles’ courage.
For Christ says, “Now my soul is troubled.” And when Paul went to the regions of Palestine, a prophet named Agabus came there and said:
Thus says the Holy Spirit: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way by the Jews in Jerusalem.”

And when all the brothers tried to restrain Paul and begged him not to go to Jerusalem, he answered in a courageous voice—or rather, in a spirit of courage and apostleship, he said to those trying to hold him back:
“What are you doing, weeping and crushing my heart within me? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of Christ.”
Paul speaks with such confidence, such boldness, such fearlessness [?], and tramples underfoot, despises, and [?] the terrors of death.
Yet Paul’s Lord said, “Now my soul is troubled.” Paul’s heart was being crushed, but was Christ troubled in his very soul?
Paul even boasted in his afflictions: “Not only this, but we also boast in our afflictions,
because we know that afflictions produce endurance.” Yet Christ, Paul’s Lord, said, “My soul is sorrowful to the point of death.” What resemblance is there to boasting?
Paul regarded his sufferings as a reason for boasting. Yet did Christ, who strengthened him, regard the dispensation as a cause for sorrow?
Consider also elsewhere how thoroughly courageous Paul’s thoughts are. Once, while he was staying in the city of Philippi, in the land of the Macedonians,
a great crowd rose up against him, and he endured all kinds of bodily torture. After inflicting many blows on him, they threw him into prison and secured his feet in the stocks.
But the valiant champion of devotion to God, and Silas, who was with him, overcame their pains through steadfastness and conquered their sufferings through courage.
The writer of the account expressed this well when he said, “At midnight Paul and Silas were praising God.” They were suffering, yet giving thanks; they were receiving blows, yet offering praise.
And notice the precision of the writer of the account. He did not say, “At midnight Paul and Silas were offering prayers to God,” but that they were praising him.
For prayers may arise from distress of heart, while praise arises from joy of heart.
There, then, they see that the apostles were expressing joy. “At midnight,” he says, “Paul and Silas were praising God.”
Praise is a sign of joyful souls. The saints, wishing to reveal the rejoicing of their souls, did not offer prayers like people in distress, but sang praises like people whose hearts were at ease.
Paul and Silas, who were human by nature, displayed courageous souls amid their sufferings. Yet do you attribute words of godlessness to Christ, who is the King of the saints?
Do you take what was said for the sake of his providential care as something that destroys his honor? Come now, turn away from such thoughts!
Let no one dishonor holy things; let no one slander the divine words; let no one strive to construct impiety from the words of the Giver of life, or regard the dispensation as a downfall.
But the listener asks us for an orderly explanation. “You have taught us well,” he says. “The words were indeed part of the dispensation. But explain also the actual significance of the dispensation.
Why did he use such words at all? Why did he say, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me’?”
“If it is possible,” brothers, introduces no necessity imposed by decrees, nor the mythical designation of birth; nor are these words of cowardice.
Nor does this accuse the speaker of any timidity. Rather, these were expressions of the dispensation in human form and of concern for those who would stumble.
For he knew that the sufferings could cause many to stumble, especially those who were unaware of the mysteries of the dispensation.
According to the saying, “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.”
Now he who manages everything with wisdom, speaking on behalf of humanity, said, “If it is possible to fulfill the saving plan in another way and complete it without death,”
so that many might not stumble because of such sufferings: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”
“But you are forcing the words,” they say. “Come, show some testimony that bears witness to the truth that he said this because of human weakness and [?].”
If that is so, listen: how was he then able, right there [?], to say to the apostle, “Pray; stay awake”? And when they fell asleep, he rebuked them and said:
“So, could you not keep watch with me for one hour? Pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.”
He did not say, “So that I do not enter.” For it was not that the sufferings would harm him, but that they would cause others to stumble. “Pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.”
He did not say, “So that we do not enter,” but, “So that you do not enter.” “I am sparing you; it is not that I wish to save myself from the sufferings.”
“I know what is to come. I am not ignorant of the saving plan that is to be fulfilled. I am no novice concerning the blessing that is to blossom for all humanity.”
“But because, even before these events take place, what you see causes you to stumble, I speak in your words: ‘If it is possible for the sufferings to pass, let them pass.’”
The words must be repeated twice and three times, to make clear that there is a possibility, not something inevitable in nature that cannot be bypassed, or an unavoidable decree, as some thought.
And do you wish to know with certainty that there was no compulsion or decree imposed from above upon the Giver of Life, but that this is his own all-knowing saving plan,
and that he accomplishes everything by his own will? Listen carefully to how the Lord himself had already dispelled the notion of compulsion and revealed the abundance of his own free will.
“No one takes my life from me,” he says. “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” And again: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up on the third day.”
And if you have authority, why do you utter such words? “If it is possible,” you say, “let this cup pass from me.”
“I say this for your sake, you who are weak, and not for my own sake, for I am strong and almighty, above and beyond every weakness.”
But why did he call the sufferings a cup? From this another question also presents itself: why did he call the sufferings a cup?
“Yes,” he says, “it is always the custom of Scripture to call the chastisement that [?] comes upon offenders a cup.” Pay close attention, and be a wise listener.
Do not seize upon the words prematurely, but listen and wait for their meaning. For someone who listens badly may interpret what is said badly.
Nevertheless, someone who speaks in the church should not consider it strange if he suffers slander from those who recklessly dare to malign him.
For the apostles were slandered as though they had said something worthless. And listen to Paul, to hear how much slander he endured in his preaching:
“Are we to say, as we are slandered and as some claim we do, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come’? Their condemnation is just.”
For those who have not heard malign others as though they had heard. What they have not heard from the teachers, they bring forward as a slander against the teachers.
But let us return to the matter before us. It is always a distinctive practice of Scripture to call the chastisements or punishments that come upon sinners a cup.
But let no enemy or spy hastily pick fault with these words and say, “Did Christ also sin, that he should bear the punishments of sinners?”
Far be it from us to say that! He owed no punishment at all. Away with that! [?] Rather, we were under punishment.
And for our sake, condemned as we were for sins and liable to punishment and torment, he took death upon himself. As Isaiah had already proclaimed and announced, he came to death for us sinners.
And that he personally accepted death on account of the punishments of sinners, let the Baptizer bear witness: “Behold the Lamb of God,
who takes away the sins of the world.” And the prophet says, “He bears our sins and suffers for us,” and, “Because of the sins of the people he came to death.”
His sufferings are called a cup, according to the words quoted earlier. For that very reason, blessed David also speaks figuratively of the punishments that will come upon sinners:
“A cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine, blended; all the sinners of the earth shall drink it.” And again, when God himself threatened the nations with punishments, he said to Jeremiah:
“Take a cup of mixed wine and give it to all the nations and to Jerusalem to drink. And say to them, ‘Drink, become drunk, and become dazed.’”
What does “become dazed” mean? Such discipline brings many into a daze, and often even into bewilderment,
especially when they see the righteous caught up together with sinners. Just so, even now people throughout the earth complain: “Why were the priests slaughtered at the altars?
Why were the holy virgins handed over to abuse? For what reason were so many evils committed, and on such a scale? Why did God not protect his own?”
And because such afflictions bring people into a daze and bewilder their minds, he rightly says, “Drink, become foolish, and run wild.”
Again, when the giver of life spoke beforehand to James and John about his sufferings, he said, “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?”
This was instead of saying, “Can you bear the sufferings that I am going to bear?” And they said, “Yes.”
But blessed David plainly showed elsewhere that death which comes upon someone for devotion to God is called a cup: “What shall I give the Lord in return for everything he has given me?”
And like a deeply grateful servant, he saw God’s benefits pouring forth all around him, and sought to give some small thing himself, willingly, in return for those boundless benefits.
It is like a poor man welcoming a rich man into his home: he becomes anxious about what he could prepare to please the rich man,
and what he could bring to the table that would be worthy of his rank. He stands perplexed and says to himself:
“What worthy thing can I find for him? What shall I do? What shall I set before him? How shall I honor him? What sort of meal can I prepare?”
In the same way, David looked at human poverty and the greatness of divine generosity, and saw that there was nothing worthy that a human being
could offer to God. He became anxious and perplexed, and gave voice to his thoughts: “What shall I give the Lord in return? I can find nothing worthy of his benefits.
What shall I give the Lord in return? What sort of person shall I become? What sacrifices shall I offer? With what [?] shall I please my benefactor?”

When he found himself lacking in everything, he discovered just one thing—and even that was worthy not in proportion to God’s generosity, but in proportion to his own willingness: “I will receive the cup of salvation.”
What is that cup? He means, “If I can bear sufferings for devotion to God, if I am able to die for [?].”
I will receive the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord. And because the saying was not clear, but concealed and abbreviated, he explains it in what follows.
I will receive the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord. He adds alongside this: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
And now, what does this saying mean: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass? Is it not clear that he was speaking of his sufferings?
But you have already been given the answer to your question: by saying, “If it is possible,” he fulfills the human aspects of the dispensation.
For the one who said this according to his humanity had himself already said according to his all-powerful divinity: I have authority to lay down my life,
and I have authority to take it up again. And he makes it clear that it was not his divinity that shrank from the sufferings, but the weakness of his flesh.
And again he says: My spirit is willing, but my flesh is weak. It was not that the sufferings would do him any harm, but that they would cause others to stumble.
And he showed this to the disciples: Remain in prayer, he says, so that you do not enter into temptation.
In another way, too, he hands down to us the very rules of prayer: not to demand outright from God the things we ask for in our prayers,
but to take refuge in him who administers everything with wisdom. For he himself says: Not as I will, but as you will.
What was fitting for him is also most appropriate for you. For when you stand in prayer, do not ask for whatever you yourself wish, but take refuge in God's will.
You too, when you stand in prayer, should speak in imitation of Christ, who humbled himself for your sake:
Not as I will, but as you will, Lord. Take refuge in God's will. Do not give him instructions, and do not regard yourself as his adviser.

For those who love God, he says, everything succeeds and will work together for their good. Whatever accords with his will is accomplished, and whatever is outside his will does not come to completion.
The cup of God's chastisement comes upon sinners as punishment. But for Christ, the sufferings were not punishment, but providence, for he endured the death of sinners without sin,
so that he might save the whole world, which had been condemned under sin. Why, he says, should death be called a cup at all?
The testimonies of Scripture themselves plainly show that punishments and death are called a cup. But why were sufferings called a cup, since a cup is in no way like death?
Because the chastisements that come upon us are harsh, unbearable, and difficult, the divine Scriptures call these afflictions a cup by analogy,
so that it may be clear that God does not torment like a harsh judge or slaughter without mercy, but heals our ailments like a physician and gives us chastisements to swallow like [?] of potent gall.
Thus the saving cup of chastisement is bitter to taste but beneficial for healing. The passage presents God as a benefactor,
who disciplines with the cup, who is benevolent like a father, and who torments and punishes like a king. He does not strike like an enemy, but causes pain like a physician.
For example, when a physician uses an iron instrument and applies cauterization to the body, he is not thereby fighting against the person, but battling the ailments.
Likewise, when God brings chastisements, he does not punish his creation, but cleanses its sins.
Have you ever seen a physician put his hand to work out of wrath, or resort to cauterization out of anger, or do anything else of the kind?
Even though the physician's face may seem terrifying to the sick person, the physician has the patient's benefit in mind.
And not because the pain-causing treatment may seem dreadful, or the promise of medical skill may be something dreadful.
Thus the blessed Paul has rightly and wonderfully set out a rule for discipline, saying, “All discipline, for a time, seems to bring not joy but sorrow.”
When the wounded man sees the physician intending to cut his wound, he considers him terrifying and flees from him as from an enemy.
But when he is healed, he then looks closely at the man from whom he once turned his face when he saw him, and bows down before him.

Do we not know that, in their anger at their pain, the sick insult their physicians, and the physician bears with those who are angry? For he knows that their insults are not deliberate, but arise from their pain.
But when they recover from their illness, they even pay those whom they considered cruel. They pay not because payment is demanded, but willingly and gladly.
In the same way, we too are now reluctant to endure afflictions; but when the fruit of those afflictions comes, then we praise our benefactor,
and in wonder we say with David, “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into rest.”
Now he calls afflictions a cup—and not simply a cup, but one in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine, yet mixed.
Again, the words seem to contain a contradiction, since mixed and unmixed are not at all alike. Why, then, should the cup be both unmixed and mixed?
For God’s judgment and the discipline that will come upon us are unmixed, and mixed while unmixed.
What is mixed in? Justice with righteousness—not lawlessness, not wrongdoing, and nothing doubtful mixed with righteousness.
Rather, the eye of judgment is truly pure and unmixed, holy and clear, strong in righteousness and radiant, keen-sighted, swift in investigation, upright in action, weighing everything, impartial.
Therefore there is a cup in the Lord’s hand containing unmixed wine, because injustice is not mixed with righteousness.
And among the adversaries there is no one who can introduce uncertainty into the judge’s truth, for there is a cup of unmixed wine in the Lord’s hand.
And if it contains unmixed wine, how can it be full and mixed? Do not let the words seem contradictory to you; rather, the truth unites them.
The cup is unmixed, as I have already said many times, because injustice is not mixed with righteousness; and it is mixed because love for humanity is also mixed with righteousness.
It is as though he were saying that it is pure in righteousness and mixed with love for humanity, for in disciplining he shows mercy, and in showing mercy he disciplines.
And see another new rule of truth: it is a sign of God’s care and love for humanity when he disciplines sinners;
a sign of goodness and wrath when he does not discipline the offender. Then [?], as though he hated you, and he turns his face away when you transgress and he does not discipline you.
“The Lord,” he says, “chastises the one he loves; he scourges every son whom he accepts.” From the one whose sins are many he turns his face away, leaving him without discipline or punishment.
And who makes this clear? God himself, through the prophet:
“Because you transgress my laws,” he says, “I will not punish your daughters when they engage in prostitution, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery.”

It is as though he were saying, “I will hand you over to your sins. I will not punish injustice, restrain corruption, or heal the wounds of transgression, but will let you die there in your wickedness.”
See how, when he is angry, he threatens not to discipline; and when he truly loves, he does not refrain from disciplining.
Thus far it has been shown, brothers, as far as we are able, what the nature of the prayer was and what he means to show by saying, “Father, if it is at all possible, let this cup pass from me.”
For such words come not from his divine majesty, but from his human dispensation.
And the Lord himself made it still clearer that I attribute the more humble words—those of fear, turmoil, and sorrow—to the weakness of the flesh.
This was to establish that he truly took flesh capable of suffering. He says, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
I repeat the saying many times to establish the meaning of the truth firmly.
Then, if anyone dares to dispute the solution to the question that we have given, let him come forward, take his stand, and fight against our arguments,
if he is capable of waging war against the divine word. Let him not [?] like an enemy, but let him fight openly, like a champion battling for the truth.
But let this be enough for now, for we have reached what lay before us at the beginning, and let us bring our discussion to rest at that same point.
It seems to me that the nature of the dispensation and the interpretation of this saying have been fully and completely explained.
For even if someone contradicts us after so much testimony, the truth will not thereby be corrupted.
As Paul also says, “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the church of God.”
For we have learned from the Scriptures to believe, not to chew the cud of speculation. And I pray to go astray with [?], rather than display cleverness with Plato.
Let what has been said be enough and sufficient for us, and let us only remember the poor. Concerning this, Paul also rightly reminded us today:

“Peter, James, and John gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.” And he immediately added to this, “Only let us remember the poor.”
Let us too remember the poor—the poor, so that we may remember ourselves. If you show mercy to another, you show mercy to yourself.
You do good to yourself if you do good to the poor. You sow for yourself and reap for yourself. Mercy is sown here, and kindness is reaped in heaven.
And do not say, “What can I do? I am bound by poverty. I wish to show mercy, but I lack the means. I desire to do good, but the scarcity of my resources does not allow it.”
Do as much as you can. Perform good deeds to the extent that you have the means.
You who are eager, learn to desire not only to listen, but also to show mercy. And listen to Isaiah: “If you give bread to the hungry with heartfelt intent.” What does “with heartfelt intent” mean?
Instead of saying, “Where will you get food to eat?” if you take and give, and let the poor person share your food, you have shown mercy to yourself by feeding him.
Do you remember? I know that you also remember the earlier things that were said about mercy.
Mercy brings about friendship with God. Mercy brings forgiveness of sins. Mercy saves from death.

Blessed Tabitha, who was handed over to death according to the laws of nature, returned once more from death to life through the gratitude of the widows. For the tears of the poor broke down the gates of death.
Consider how much the prayers of the poor can accomplish. When Tabitha, who was full of good works, died, all the widows came and stood around Peter, weeping.
And the tears of the poor quieted their grief—or rather, conquered the very tyranny of death. For she who had died according to the laws of nature returned again through the word of grace.
She was full of compassion and good works. The widows wept and appealed to God. Dying is according to our nature, but raising the dead is outside and above our nature.
For if the tears of the poor could accomplish what is beyond our nature, could they not accomplish what is according to nature?

Consider how powerful a widow’s cries are when she cries out against a rich man. If a poor person cries out against a powerful man who oppresses him, if an orphan cries out against [?], what vengeance will their cries bring about?

Do not let the poor person cry out against you, or the needy person groan, or the orphan lament and raise a complaint against you. Instead, sow mercy among orphans, so that you may store up kindness for your own children.
Be an imitator of Abraham, who spread compassionate kindness among all who were in need and left his descendants a pledge of salvation.
And see the wonderful thing: because of the honor he showed through hospitality, he was found worthy to receive even the angels of God.
He received the angels with hospitality, thinking they were human beings. Afterward he learned that they were angels, and with them he saw God.
And because he loved hospitality, God gave him an inexhaustible table in return.
For during the forty years when the people descended from him were strangers in the wilderness, God fed them abundantly, preparing a table for them in the wilderness.
He gave his children food produced without human labor for forty years in the wilderness, and fed the people descended from Abraham because of Abraham’s hospitable table.

And because the shade of the tree gave relief from the heat to many poor people, a sheltering cloud gave relief from the heat to the people, and carefully preserved the branches that sprang from the God-fearing root.
And see the wonders—what a repayment he made! Human beings ate the bread of angels. Indeed, the two things were closely alike.
For Abraham also received the angels. Because the angels ate the [?] of human beings, human beings in turn ate the food of angels.
For hospitality advances in just this way: by receiving human beings, one comes to receive angels as well, and from being a host to angels,
one comes to be a host to God as well. For it was God who had the angels as servants accompanying him as a guest.
Therefore our Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, when he spoke about the fruit of a kindly table, said, “Whoever receives you receives me.”
Thus blessed Abraham also received God through his hospitality.
And see the wonderful thing: he saw three, but bowed down to only one. For he did not say, “Lords,” but “Lord.” He saw three, but blessed the one.
But now is not the time to examine that closely, but to present the teaching about hospitality, since he received them and gave them rest.
See the new designs of God’s kindness, and what debts the loving God repays:
“I am,” he says, “the God of the fathers, who came down from heaven. You fed the heavenly beings, and I will give heavenly food to your descendants.”
Contrary to the nature of angels, angels ate human food; and beyond the [?] of human beings, human beings partake of heavenly bread.
This food is not familiar to the nature of angels, nor was that food suited to human nature. But now is not the time to present this precisely and [?].
But you must long for a life of hospitality and fight the good fight for the poor, so that you may store up treasure for yourself.
You have the handles of the plow: sow in the fields of the needy. “He distributed,” it says, “and gave to [?]; his righteousness endures forever.”

Let this much suffice, for this renewed reminder about the poor was not intended as instruction but as confirmation; the things already said at first were enough to encourage those with trained minds.
Let us now await our spiritual father, who is a true teacher of the church, and let us also say to him at the proper time, “Awake,
my glory! Awake, psaltery and harp!” For we need your teaching and your fatherly voice to confirm these words of ours.
Although there is much flour, a little leaven is also needed. Although we have spoken many words,
we still need your fatherly help to lend weight to and confirm our words, to the glory of Christ our God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
